title: Design a Notification System
summary: End-to-end system design of a multi-channel notification platform (push, SMS, email, in-app) covering requirements, architecture, templates, preferences, priority queues, retries, dedup, rate limiting, providers, delivery tracking, and scaling trade-offs.

chapters.title: Notification System Design Cover
points: Scope and requirements
High-level architecture
Channels and providers
Templates and preferences
Priority queues and workers
Retries, DLQ, dedup
Rate limiting
Delivery tracking
Scaling and interview Q&A

chapters.title: Problem Statement, Scope and Requirements
points: Scope: push (APNs/FCM), SMS, email, in-app; triggered by services, scheduled, or bulk campaigns; out of scope: marketing UI, content authoring
Functional: send single/bulk, template rendering, per-user opt-in/out per channel and category, scheduling, delivery status query
Scale estimate: 10M DAU, 5 notifications/user/day = 50M/day, about 580 QPS average, 5k QPS peak (10x burst)
Latency targets: OTP/critical under 2s end to end; transactional under 10s; marketing within minutes
Non-functional: at-least-once delivery, 99.95% availability, no loss after accept (durable ack), idempotent sends
Storage estimate: 50M events/day x 1 KB = 50 GB/day, 90-day retention = about 4.5 TB

chapters.title: High-Level Architecture (Notification System)
points: Flow: producer service -> Notification API -> validator/dedup/preference check -> priority Kafka topics -> channel workers -> provider adapters -> provider
Separate queue per channel and per priority so a slow SMS provider cannot block push
Synchronous accept (202 + notification_id), asynchronous delivery
Stateless API and workers scale horizontally; Kafka partitioned by user_id preserves per-user ordering
Components: Template Service, Preference Service, Rate Limiter (Redis), Scheduler, Tracking Service, Dead Letter Queue
Build vs buy: own pipeline plus providers (Twilio, SES, FCM) beats a single vendor for cost and failover

chapters.title: Notification API and Intake Service
points: Responsibilities: authenticate producer, validate payload, assign notification_id, enqueue, return 202
POST /v1/notifications {user_id, template_id, channel[], priority, idempotency_key, data}; GET /v1/notifications/{id}
Flow: validate -> idempotency check (Redis SETNX, 24h TTL) -> write outbox row -> publish to Kafka -> ack
Table notifications(id, user_id, template_id, priority, status, idempotency_key UNIQUE, created_at); partition by created_at
Failure: Kafka down -> transactional outbox plus relay retries so accepted events are never lost
Metrics: accept p99 under 50 ms, 5xx rate under 0.1%, enqueue lag, rejected-by-validation rate

chapters.title: Templates and Localization Service
points: Responsibilities: store versioned templates per channel and locale, render variables, enforce size limits (SMS 160 GSM-7 chars, push payload 4 KB)
Render at worker time using template_id + version + data; cache compiled templates in memory, TTL 5 min
Table templates(id, version, channel, locale, subject, body, status draft/active); locale fallback en
API: POST /templates, PUT /templates/{id}/versions, GET /templates/{id}?locale=hi
Failure: missing variable -> fail fast to DLQ with reason, never send a literal {{name}}
Metrics: render p99 under 5 ms, cache hit rate above 95%, render error rate

chapters.title: User Preferences and Opt-Out
points: Responsibilities: per-user, per-channel, per-category opt-in, quiet hours with timezone, global unsubscribe, legal opt-out (TCPA, CAN-SPAM)
Check order: global opt-out -> channel enabled -> category enabled -> quiet hours -> device token valid
Table user_prefs(user_id, channel, category, enabled, quiet_start, quiet_end, tz); device_tokens(user_id, token, platform, last_seen)
API: GET/PUT /v1/users/{id}/preferences; unsubscribe link with signed token
Failure: preference store down -> critical (OTP) fails open, marketing fails closed; Redis cache 10 min TTL, invalidate on write
Metrics: cache hit rate, opt-out rate, suppressed-by-preference count, stale invalid token rate

chapters.title: Priority Queues and Channel Workers
points: Responsibilities: isolate traffic by priority (critical, high, normal, bulk) so a campaign never delays an OTP
Kafka topics per channel x priority; workers weight consumption 8:4:2:1 or run dedicated consumer groups for critical
Flow: consume -> preference check -> render -> rate limit -> provider call -> emit status event -> commit offset
Bulk campaigns fan out via a batch job into the bulk topic at throttled rate (for example 2k msgs/sec)
Failure: worker crash -> offset uncommitted -> redelivery; consumer lag alert triggers autoscaling
Metrics: consumer lag per topic, queue wait p99 (critical under 500 ms), worker throughput, autoscale events

chapters.title: Retries, Dead Letters and Deduplication
points: Retry only transient errors (5xx, timeout, 429); never retry permanent ones (invalid token, 400, unsubscribed)
Exponential backoff with jitter: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s... capped at 5 attempts, via delay topics retry-1m, retry-5m, retry-30m
After max attempts move to DLQ with error payload; replay tool re-injects after fix; alert if DLQ depth above 100
Dedup key = hash(user_id, template_id, idempotency_key) in Redis SET NX EX 24h; blocks duplicate sends on producer retry
At-least-once plus dedup gives effectively-once; exactly-once is impossible across a provider boundary, so pass provider idempotency key where supported
Metrics: retry rate under 5%, DLQ rate under 0.1%, duplicate-suppressed count, time-to-success after retry

chapters.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
points: Per-user limit: for example 5 marketing push/day and 3 SMS/hour via Redis token bucket or sliding window keyed user:channel:category
Critical categories (OTP, security alerts) bypass per-user caps but have their own abuse limit (5 OTPs/10 min)
Per-provider limit: stay under vendor caps (for example SES 14 emails/sec per account tier, Twilio 1 msg/sec per number) with a global token bucket
Token bucket vs sliding window: bucket allows bursts and O(1) memory; sliding window is stricter but costs more memory
Over-limit action: drop, delay to a later window, or digest; Redis down -> fail open for critical, fail closed for bulk
Metrics: throttled count by rule, 429 from providers, limiter p99 under 2 ms

chapters.title: Third-Party Providers and Failover
points: Provider adapter interface send(msg) -> {provider_id, status}, one adapter each for FCM, APNs, Twilio, SES, SendGrid
Push: APNs (iOS) and FCM (Android/web) with token per device; SMS: Twilio, Vonage; email: SES (cheap, about $0.10 per 1k), SendGrid
Failover: circuit breaker per provider (open after 50% errors over 30s), route to secondary provider, half-open probe after 60s
Prune invalid tokens on APNs 410 / FCM UNREGISTERED responses
Failure: provider outage -> breaker opens, queue buffers, retries drain after recovery; routing weights by cost and deliverability
Metrics: provider success rate above 99%, p99 provider latency, cost per 1k messages, failover count

chapters.title: Delivery Tracking and In-App Inbox
points: Status lifecycle: queued -> sent -> delivered -> opened -> clicked, or failed / suppressed / bounced
Sources: provider webhooks (SES SNS, Twilio status callback), device ack for push open, tracking pixel and redirect links for email
Table notification_events(notification_id, status, ts, provider, error) append-only in Cassandra/ClickHouse; current status cached in Redis
In-app inbox: table inbox(user_id, notif_id, read, created_at) keyed by user_id, delivered live over WebSocket/SSE, unread count in Redis
API: GET /v1/notifications/{id}/events; GET /v1/users/{id}/inbox?cursor=; POST /inbox/{id}/read
Failure: webhooks are out of order or duplicated -> upsert by status rank; missed webhook -> poll provider after 15 min; metrics: delivery rate above 98%, open rate, webhook lag under 30s

chapters.title: Scaling, Failure Handling, Trade-offs and Interview Questions
points: Scale: 5k QPS peak needs about 20 API pods and 50 workers; Kafka 100 partitions per hot topic; shard Redis by user_id
Trade-off: at-least-once + dedup versus exactly-once; push (low latency) versus pull (reliable fan-out for inbox)
Multi-region active-active: route producers to the nearest region, dedup keys replicated, provider failover per region
Mistakes: single shared queue for all priorities, retrying permanent errors, no idempotency key, sending in user's quiet hours, ignoring token cleanup
Interview Q: how to avoid duplicates on retry, how to prevent OTP delay during a campaign, how to handle a provider outage
Cheatsheet: 202 accept -> outbox -> Kafka per channel x priority -> prefs -> render -> limit -> adapter -> track; backoff 1s-8s x5 then DLQ
